fetched_contents.text: Mechanisms controlling green roof peak flow rate attenuation Introduction Rapid stormwater drainage from impervious surfaces in urban areas increases stress on municipal infrastructure and downstream environments (e.g. channel erosion and increased flooding). Green roofs are a low impact development (LID) tool that can mitigate excessive stormwater drainage and its impacts (Dhalla and Zimmer, 2010). They are generally comprised of a waterproofing membrane and a drainage layer that is overlain by growing medium and vegetation. In addition to retaining stormwater and thus reducing the volume of stormwater, green roofs can attenuate (i.e., reduce peak flow rates) and delay peak stormwater flow rates (Dhalla and Zimmer, 2010, P’ng and Henry, 2003). Reduced flow rates decrease downstream environmental damage, while peak run off delay reduces the total peak sewer flow rates by delaying the contribution from a green roof relative to runoff from impervious surfaces. The stormwater management benefits that green roofs provide are now recognized by several large cities. For instance, the City of Toronto (Canada) requires a green roof on any newly constructed building with a floor area over 2000 m2 (Borooah and Aster, 2007, Toronto Municipal Code Chapter 492, Green Roofs, 2017). With the increasing implementation of green roofs, detailed knowledge of how green roofs attenuate and delay peak flow rates is essential to optimize their performance as a stormwater management tool. The hydrology of a green roof is governed by unsaturated soil conditions. Assuming homogenous green roof growth media when precipitation falls on a green roof, rain is held in the growing medium through capillary storage until field capacity is reached, at which point drainage occurs. Fig. 1 illustrates the water storage and drainage response of a green roof during two typical rain events. Field capacity is defined in a variety of ways in the soil literature but is commonly considered as the threshold below which soil water flux out of the rooting zone is negligible for deep soil profiles (Assouline and Or, 2014, Twarakavi et al., 2009). As it relates to green roofs, we consider field capacity to be the point at which soil capillary pressure can no longer retain water in the medium. This concept of field capacity is indicated in Fig. 1. The intersection of the horizontal and vertical dashed lines indicates the storage capacity and time at which there is no more capillary storage available and field capacity is reached. In Fig. 1a there are three clear rainfall peaks. The first two peaks are almost completely attenuated (i.e., very little or no drainage from single green roof modules or from the full green roof), but once field capacity is reached the peak attenuation response (i.e., extent to which peak outflow is reduced relative to peak inflow) changes considerably. It is noted that there is some drainage before field capacity is reached for the September 11th 2013 rainfall event shown in Fig. 1(b). This is likely a result of preferential flow paths present in the growth medium as has been reported in other studies (Liu and Fassman-Beck, 2016, Zhang et al., 2018). While the concept of field capacity has received some attention in green roof experimental monitoring (Akther et al., 2018, Bengtsson, 2005, Villarreal, 2007, Villarreal and Bengtsson, 2005, Zhang et al., 2018) and modelling studies (Hilten et al., 2008, She and Pang, 2010), field capacity has generally only been considered in the context of the extent to which the green roof can retain precipitation volume. As such the importance of field capacity on peak flow rate attenuation and delay (Fig. 1) requires more investigation, quantitative understanding and simulation of its impact to improve field design. Fig. 1a also illustrates the effect of gravity storage. The term gravity storage is used to describe transient water retention in the medium due to short-lived imbalance between free drainage from the base of the module and rainfall intensity. Gravity storage occurs once field capacity is reached and the force applied by gravity overcomes the ability of soil capillaries to retain water, providing only temporary storage. The effects of gravity storage are not well quantified for green roofs. Bengtsson (2005) examined gravity storage using artificial rainfall experiments conducted by saturating one 4 × 1.25 m green roof plot and letting it drain to field capacity. They found gravity storage varied with rain intensity; 1 mm/min rain resulted in almost 8 mm of gravity storage, compared with only 4 mm of gravity storage when the rain intensity was reduced to 0.4 mm/min. In these experiments gravity storage was not directly measured but it was inferred from the experimental difference between rainfall and measured drainage rates. Results from the 1.8 m2 experimental green roof study of Palla et al. (2011) also suggest that gravity storage leads to peak flow rate attenuation >40%. Gravity storage has a lower attenuation potential than capillary storage, but it is important to quantify the effects of gravity storage to improve design of green roofs for large storms or under wet conditions. Numerous studies have investigated green roof stormwater performance (Berardi et al., 2014, Berndtsson, 2010). The volumetric retention of stormwater (i.e., the difference in area under the rainfall curve and drainage curve in Fig. 1) has been found to range from 27 to 81% for extensive green roofs (Mentens et al., 2006). While many studies have quantified stormwater retention, there is a need for an improved mechanistic understanding of the attenuation and delay of peak stormwater drainage from green roofs (Johannessen et al., 2019, Shafique et al., 2018). fetched_contents.text: The effects of large-scale green roof implementation on the rainfall-runoff in a tropical urbanized subcatchment by Jim van Spengen MSc thesis report The hydrological effects of urbanization affect the rainfall-runoff regime of many cities in the world. While traditional stormwater drainage systems are often able to effectively serve the function of flood control, they increase downstream peak flows and do not provide a habitat to support a healthy aquatic ecosystem. In order to improve this situation, water managers introduced the concept of Low Impact Development. The main purpose of Low Impact Development is to mimic predevelopment site hydrology as much as possible, by reducing the volume and peak rate of flow, controlling the water quality and promoting the recharge of stormwater with decentralized, on-site detention. Green roofs are an interesting Low Impact Development measure with great large-scale implementation potential in existing urban areas as well as in areas with new housing development, because roofs account for 20-50% of the total urban land cover. This research was initiated by a lack of knowledge related to the quantitative hydrological effects of green roofs in the tropics. Singapore was chosen as a case study for this research. The main goals of the research are 1) to analyze the effects of green roofs on the rainfall-runoff in Singapore and 2) to determine the quantitative hydrological contribution of large-scale green roof implementation to sustainable stormwater drainage systems in Singapore. Methodology To achieve these goals a research approach is used, which combines green roof experiment measurements with green roof model simulations. First, an approach to measure and simulate the rainfall-runoff processes that occur on 1 m2 experiment platforms has been set up. Runoff data from an extensive green roof platform, with a 12 cm soil media, and a reference roof were analyzed for 66 rainfall events in four periods of one month. Retention, peak discharge reduction, detention and base flow variables and performance indicators were used to quantify the hydrological effects of green roofs. An unsaturated zone model for the simulation of green roof rainfall-runoff was conceptualized and specified in the physically based HYDRUS-1D simulation software, which numerically solves the Richards equation for water flow in variably saturated porous media. A 9.4 ha subcatchment was used as a case study in order to quantify the hydrological effects of large-scale green roof implementation on the rainfall-runoff in Singapore. Based on a conceptualized representation of the Sunset Way subcatchment, a hydraulic routing model was build in the SOBEK software package. As in other available commercial hydraulic models, an explicit green roof modelling option is not available in the current SOBEK software. Therefore, this thesis presents a methodology that couples pre-processed green roof runoff from the HYDRUS-1D model to the SOBEK model for an accurate simulation of the scaled-up green roof effects in the case study area. Results Analysis of experiment measurements shows that the green roof platform retained 39% (234 mm) more rainfall than a reference roof and reduces the peak discharge with 64% compared to the reference roof. The average time to peak of the green roof hydrograph appeared 34 minutes after the reference roof peak and green roof platforms provided an average additional base flow runoff of 0.41 liters/m2 . However, average experiment performance values do not give practical implications whether green roofs are an effective stormwater management solution. Individual event analysis shows that green roofs do not simply absorb water and slowly release it over a period of time. Instead, retention is the primary function of green roofs: rainfall is retained until the maximum storage capacity of the soil media. Detention and peak discharge reduction is provided by green roofs until the moment of soil saturation. After this moment, green roof peak detention is limited to 1-2 minutes and runoff intensities closely follow the rainfall and reference roof intensities. Base flow conservation by extensive green roofs is not provided for rainfall events that are nearly or totally retained. If green roofs get saturated during the rainfall event, minor base flow conservation was observed for up to 3 hours after the last rainfall. Several laboratory and field experiments were performed in order to provide a physically based initial set of parameters for the HYDRUS-1D model. Four unique optimized parameter vectors for the hydraulic functions of van Genuchten were determined with inverse modelling of transient flow experiments. It was shown that runoff at the bottom of a green roof can be described with a seepage face boundary. Runoff starts or stops when the soil water content at the bottom respectively exceeds or drops below a threshold value of 0.61. The physical background of the model provided a better understanding of the hydrological processes and the soil physics in a green roof media. Simulation results of twelve rainfall-runoff events in September, 2009 (calibration period) and December, 2009 (validation period) show that the HYDRUS-1D model gives an accurate representation of the measured green roof runoff characteristics on event scale. A limitation of the model is the over prediction of the green roof runoff when events quickly follow-up. fetched_contents.text: Soak Up the Rain: Green Roofs Green roofs have a layer of plant material that absorbs water like a sponge. They capture water when it rains, slowly releasing it through evaporation and plant use. Green roofs can significantly reduce the amount of rain water that would otherwise run off an impervious roof surface. Green roofs can also help reduce building energy usage and noise levels while increasing the durability and lifespan of the roof compared to conventional roofs. Green roofs are being increasingly used in urban areas where space constraints limit the use of other stormwater management practices. Note: Structures must be able to support the loading of green roof materials under fully saturated conditions. Green roofs reduce peak water flow during rainfall by delaying runoff, reducing immediate runoff volume, and lowering peak discharge. The evidence points to a combination of interception, storage, evapotranspiration, and infiltration as the primary mechanisms.

First, interception and storage delay runoff by temporarily holding rainfall on the green roof surface and within the growing medium. The ScienceDirect study explains that green roofs “retain stormwater and thus reduce the volume of stormwater,” and that water is held in the growing medium through capillary storage until field capacity is reached, after which drainage occurs [N1-F1]. It also notes that gravity storage temporarily retains water once field capacity is reached, further delaying outflow [N1-F1]. A separate source says green roofs can “temporarily retain rainwater through infiltration” and “delay the peak time of runoff” [N1-R2]. This means that rainfall is not immediately converted into surface runoff; instead, it is intercepted and stored, reducing the immediate contribution to downstream flow.

Second, infiltration and surface retention reduce the immediate volume of runoff. The same ScienceDirect article states that green roofs can “reduce the total volume of runoff by 60–100%” depending on the type of green roof used [N1-R5], and another source says green roofs “alleviate potential damage from heavy rainfall by delaying the peak time of runoff, temporarily retaining rainwater through infiltration” [N1-R2]. In practical terms, this means green roofs reduce the amount of water that enters the sewer or drainage system right away, which helps lower the immediate peak discharge.

Third, green roofs can lower peak discharge and shift runoff timing. The ScienceDirect study explicitly says green roofs can “attenuate (i.e., reduce peak flow rates) and delay peak stormwater flow rates” [N1-F1]. It also states that “peak run off delay reduces the total peak sewer flow rates by delaying the contribution from a green roof relative to runoff from impervious surfaces” [N1-F1]. Another source reports that green roofs can reduce peak discharge by 64% compared to a reference roof in a Singapore case study, while also increasing the average time to peak by 34 minutes [N2-F2]. This shows not only lower peak discharge but also a shifted timing of runoff, which can help reduce the stress on drainage systems during intense rainfall.

Taken together, the modeling and mechanistic evidence supports a layered explanation: interception and storage delay runoff, infiltration and retention reduce immediate runoff volume, and green roofs lower peak discharge while shifting runoff timing [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-F2].

Green roofs fit into urban drainage and flood control systems as part of low-impact development (LID) and stormwater management strategies. The evidence frames them as a tool to “mitigate excessive stormwater drainage and its impacts” [N1-F1], and the US EPA states green roofs “can significantly reduce the amount of rain water that would otherwise run off an impervious roof surface” [N3-F3]. In urban contexts, green roofs are especially valuable where space constraints limit other stormwater management practices [N3-F3]. They also fit into broader LID systems, including green infrastructure such as permeable pavement, bioretention, bioswales, and detention basins [N6-R1]. The EPA’s broader discussion of green infrastructure emphasizes that green roofs are part of a suite of nature-based solutions used to reduce stormwater runoff and manage flood risk [N3-F3].

The trade-offs between flood reduction, water quality, and other benefits are partly implied by the evidence. Green roofs are clearly positioned as a stormwater management tool, but the evidence also shows that their benefits depend on design, installation, and management. The ScienceDirect study notes that retention capacity typically ranges from 40–80% [N5-F4], and that “the proven efficiency of green roofs depends on numerous factors” [N5-F4]. The same source warns that extrapolating test results from one region to another carries a larger risk of error [N5-F4]. In addition, the Singapore case study highlights that green roofs can reduce peak discharge and delay runoff, but also notes that model results can be limited by assumptions and that the contribution of green roofs may depend on design storm conditions [N2-F2]. This suggests that while green roofs can reduce flood risk, their effectiveness is not automatic and must be balanced against practical constraints.

The evidence also indicates when green roofs are most valuable versus when they are less effective. They are most valuable in dense urban areas where impervious surfaces dominate and where rooftop area can be used to capture and retain stormwater [N3-F3]. They are especially effective when the goal is to reduce peak discharge and delay runoff, as shown by the Singapore case study’s 64% peak discharge reduction and 34-minute delay in time to peak [N2-F2]. In contrast, the evidence suggests they may be less effective under very high rainfall volumes or when the roof is not designed to retain enough water. The scale dynamics study says green roof drainage area has the greatest impact on peak runoff reduction, while retention and peak reduction decrease with increased rainfall volume [N4-R1]. The same study also states that the minimum media depth should be 4 inches for non-irrigated roofs, highlighting that design and installation factors strongly influence effectiveness [N4-R2]. In short, green roofs are most valuable when integrated into urban stormwater systems with appropriate design, management, and scale, but their benefits may be limited when rainfall is extreme or when installation factors are inadequate [N3-F3][N5-F4][N4-R1][N4-R2].

The real-world urban studies evidence shows measurable flood risk reduction in specific cities and storm events, with clear quantitative effects on peak flow and rainfall intensity. The strongest case study provided is the Singapore rooftop-scale study, which reports that an extensive green roof retained 39% more rainfall than a reference roof and reduced peak discharge by 64% compared to the reference roof [N2-F2]. The same study also found that the average time to peak for the green roof hydrograph was 34 minutes after the reference roof peak [N2-F2]. This indicates a measurable flood risk reduction effect under typical rainfall events, even though the authors caution that average experiment values do not always translate directly to practical effectiveness [N2-F2]. 

Another case study from Tehran is mentioned in the search evidence, though the excerpt is limited and does not provide specific peak flow reduction numbers [N2-R1]. The Singapore study is therefore the clearest example of a measurable urban flood risk reduction effect. The broader evidence also points to the importance of rainfall intensity and event characteristics. The Singapore study notes that retention and peak reduction decrease with increased rainfall volume [N4-R1], while another study found a weak correlation between peak flow rate and rainfall intensity [N4-R3]. This suggests that green roofs can reduce flood risk, but the magnitude of reduction depends on how intense the rainfall is.

On the question of how much peak flow was reduced and under what rainfall intensities, the evidence is strongest for the Singapore case study. The study reports 64% peak discharge reduction compared to the reference roof, with a 34-minute delay in time to peak [N2-F2]. The scale dynamics study adds that green roof drainage area has the greatest impact on peak runoff reduction, and that retention and peak reduction decrease with increased rainfall volume [N4-R1]. This implies that under higher-intensity storms or larger rainfall volumes, the relative benefit of green roofs may be smaller. The evidence also shows that some events may not produce the same level of flood risk reduction: the Singapore study found that green roofs do not simply absorb water and slowly release it over time, and that retention is the primary function until soil saturation is reached [N2-F2]. After saturation, peak detention is limited to 1–2 minutes, and runoff intensities closely follow rainfall intensity [N2-F2]. This matters because flood risk reduction is not uniform across all storms.

Installation and management factors that influenced effectiveness are also clear. The minimum media depth for non-irrigated roofs is reported as 4 inches, and for irrigated roofs 3 inches [N4-R2]. The Singapore study emphasizes that retention capacity typically ranges from 40–80% [N5-F4], and that the proven efficiency of green roofs depends on numerous factors [N5-F4]. The same study warns that extrapolating results from one region to another carries a larger risk of error [N5-F4]. The case study also shows that green roofs can be implemented on rooftops of different sizes and that their effects depend on the hydrological processes of the roof media, including infiltration, storage, and drainage [N2-F2]. In short, effectiveness depends on roof design, media depth, vegetation type, and whether the roof is saturated during the event [N4-R2][N5-F4][N2-F2].

Modeling helps quantify and compare green roof flood mitigation by simulating peak flow prediction, comparing green roofs against other infrastructure, and identifying scale- and design-dependent effects. The evidence shows that green roof performance is often modeled using SWMM and related LID controls, and that model results can be used to estimate runoff reduction and peak discharge effects.

For peak flow prediction, the evidence indicates that models rely on rainfall inputs, green roof design parameters, and hydrological assumptions about storage, infiltration, and drainage. The SWMM modeling study explicitly says the storm water performance was simulated using SWMM with Low Impact Development (LID) Controls, and notes that the model consists of many parameters for a particular layer of green roofs [N5-F4]. Another source states that SWMM allows simulating runoff from green and grey roofs with a good fit between observed and simulated runoff, though in some cases simulation results were unsatisfactory and the Nash coefficient had negative values [N5-F4]. This suggests that model inputs include rainfall, green roof media properties, vegetation, and drainage layer characteristics, but also that model assumptions and calibration are important for accuracy.

Model results can be used to compare green roofs with other infrastructure. The modeling study notes that green roofs can “better manage peak flows in the most critical events” when detention-based practices are incorporated [N5-R2]. It also mentions that green and grey roofs can equally reduce the maximum flow by 17% in one study [N5-R5]. This implies that models can compare green roofs against other stormwater control measures, such as detention basins, permeable pavement, and grey roofs, and that the relative effectiveness may vary depending on the event and design. The modeling evidence also shows that model results can be sensitive to assumptions and parameter choices, as the SWMM study found that the complexity of the LID module did not improve accuracy and that further research was needed to determine the role of roof slope, vegetation cover, and drying processes [N5-F4].

Modeling is especially useful for identifying scale-dependent and design-dependent effects. The scale dynamics study finds that green roof drainage area has the greatest impact on peak runoff reduction, and that retention and peak reduction decrease with increased rainfall volume [N4-R1]. Another source reports that the addition of just 3.8 cm of storage can result in a 38.6% reduction in peak discharge for a rainfall depth of 50 mm [N7-R3]. This shows that modeling can reveal how design choices—such as media depth, storage capacity, and roof area—change flood mitigation outcomes. The evidence also indicates that modeling can help compare rooftop-scale performance with larger catchment effects, as the Singapore study used a 9.4 ha subcatchment to scale up the green roof effects [N2-F2]. Overall, modeling helps quantify green roof flood mitigation by predicting peak flow, comparing with other infrastructure, and identifying how design and scale affect performance [N5-F4][N5-R2][N5-R5][N4-R1][N7-R3][N2-F2].

## Integrated explanation: how green roofs help reduce peak water flow and flooding risks during heavy rainfall

Green roofs help reduce peak water flow and flooding risks during heavy rainfall by acting as a natural stormwater buffer in urban areas. They do this through a combination of mechanisms: **interception and storage delay runoff**, **infiltration and surface retention reduce immediate runoff volume**, and **green roofs lower peak discharge while shifting runoff timing** [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-F2]. In dense urban environments where impervious surfaces dominate, this can significantly reduce the stress on drainage systems and lower the risk of localized flooding [N3-F3][N1-F1].

### 1) Mechanisms by which green roofs reduce peak water flow

Green roofs reduce peak water flow by temporarily holding rainfall and delaying its release into the drainage system. The evidence shows that water is intercepted and stored in the growing medium, where capillary storage holds water until field capacity is reached, after which drainage begins [N1-F1]. Gravity storage can also temporarily retain water once field capacity is reached, providing further delay [N1-F1]. This means that rainfall does not immediately become runoff; instead, it is intercepted and stored, reducing the immediate contribution to downstream flow [N1-R2].

In addition to delaying runoff, green roofs reduce the immediate volume of runoff. The ScienceDirect study notes that green roofs can “reduce the total volume of runoff by 60–100%” depending on the type of green roof used [N1-R5], and another source says they “temporarily retain rainwater through infiltration” and “delay the peak time of runoff” [N1-R2]. In practical terms, this means green roofs lower the volume of water that enters the sewer or drainage system right away, which helps reduce peak discharge.

Green roofs can also lower peak discharge and shift runoff timing. The same ScienceDirect article explicitly states that green roofs can “attenuate (i.e., reduce peak flow rates) and delay peak stormwater flow rates” [N1-F1]. It also says peak runoff delay reduces the total peak sewer flow rates by delaying the contribution from a green roof relative to runoff from impervious surfaces [N1-F1]. The Singapore case study provides a concrete example: an extensive green roof reduced peak discharge by 64% compared to a reference roof and increased the average time to peak by 34 minutes [N2-F2]. This shows not only lower peak discharge but also a delayed peak, which can help reduce the intensity of flow entering drainage systems during intense rainfall [N2-F2].

### 2) Real-world evidence from urban studies

The real-world evidence shows that green roofs can produce measurable flood risk reduction in specific cities and storm events. It also says peak runoff delay reduces the total peak sewer flow rates by delaying the contribution from a green roof relative to runoff from impervious surfaces [N1-F1]. ## Integrated explanation: how green roofs help reduce peak water flow and flooding risks during heavy rainfall

Green roofs help reduce peak water flow and flooding risks during heavy rainfall by acting as a natural stormwater buffer in urban areas. They do this through a combination of mechanisms: **interception and storage delay runoff**, **infiltration and surface retention reduce immediate runoff volume**, and **green roofs lower peak discharge while shifting runoff timing** [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-F2]. In dense urban environments where impervious surfaces dominate, this can significantly reduce the stress on drainage systems and lower the risk of localized flooding [N3-F3][N1-F1].

### 1) Mechanisms by which green roofs reduce peak water flow

Green roofs reduce peak water flow by temporarily holding rainfall and delaying its release into the drainage system. The evidence shows that water is intercepted and stored in the growing medium, where capillary storage holds water until field capacity is reached, after which drainage begins [N1-F1]. Gravity storage can also temporarily retain water once field capacity is reached, providing further delay [N1-F1]. This means that rainfall does not immediately become runoff; instead, it is intercepted and stored, reducing the immediate contribution to downstream flow [N1-R2].

In addition to delaying runoff, green roofs reduce the immediate volume of runoff. The ScienceDirect study notes that green roofs can “reduce the total volume of runoff by 60–100%” depending on the type of green roof used [N1-R5], and another source says they “temporarily retain rainwater through infiltration” and “delay the peak time of runoff” [N1-R2]. In practical terms, this means green roofs lower the volume of water that enters the sewer or drainage system right away, which helps reduce peak discharge.

Green roofs can also lower peak discharge and shift runoff timing. The same ScienceDirect article explicitly states that green roofs can “attenuate (i.e., reduce peak flow rates) and delay peak stormwater flow rates” [N1-F1]. It also says peak runoff delay reduces the total peak sewer flow rates by delaying the contribution from a green roof relative to runoff from impervious surfaces [N1-F1]. The Singapore case study provides a concrete example: an extensive green roof reduced peak discharge by 64% compared to a reference roof and increased the average time to peak by 34 minutes [N2-F2]. This shows not only lower peak discharge but also a delayed peak, which can help reduce the intensity of flow entering drainage systems during intense rainfall [N2-F2].

### 2) Real-world evidence from urban studies

The real-world evidence shows that green roofs can produce measurable flood risk reduction in specific cities and storm events. The strongest case study provided is Singapore, where an extensive green roof retained 39% more rainfall than a reference roof and reduced peak discharge by 64% [N2-F2]. The study also found that the average time to peak for the green roof hydrograph was 34 minutes after the reference roof peak [N2-F2]. These are direct quantitative demonstrations of flood risk reduction under typical rainfall conditions [N2-F2].

Other studies and case studies are also relevant. The search evidence includes a Tehran urban flood management case study, though the excerpt does not provide specific peak flow numbers [N2-R1]. A broader scale dynamics study found that green roof drainage area has the greatest impact on peak runoff reduction, while retention and peak reduction decrease with increased rainfall volume [N4-R1]. Another study found a weak correlation between peak flow rate and rainfall intensity [N4-R3]. Taken together, this suggests that green roofs can reduce flood risk, but the magnitude of reduction depends on the storm event and how intense the rainfall is [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R3].

The evidence also indicates when green roofs are most valuable versus when they are less effective. They are most valuable in dense urban areas where impervious surfaces dominate and where rooftop area can be used to capture and retain stormwater [N3-F3]. In contrast, the evidence suggests they may be less effective under very high rainfall volumes or when the roof is not designed to retain enough water. The scale dynamics study explicitly says retention and peak reduction decrease with increased rainfall volume [N4-R1], while the Singapore study notes that after soil saturation, peak detention is limited to 1–2 minutes and runoff intensities closely follow rainfall intensity [N2-F2]. This matters because flood risk reduction is not uniform across all storms.

Installation and management factors strongly influence effectiveness. The minimum media depth for non-irrigated roofs is reported as 4 inches, and for irrigated roofs 3 inches [N4-R2]. The broader evidence also indicates that retention capacity typically ranges from 40–80% [N5-F4], and that the proven efficiency of green roofs depends on numerous factors [N5-F4]. The Singapore study warns that extrapolating results from one region to another carries a larger risk of error [N5-F4]. So, effectiveness depends on roof design, media depth, vegetation type, and whether the roof is saturated during the event [N4-R2][N5-F4][N2-F2].

### 3) Urban context and broader stormwater management implications

In urban stormwater management, green roofs fit into low-impact development (LID) and broader stormwater management systems as part of a suite of nature-based solutions [N3-F3][N1-F1]. The US EPA notes that green roofs can significantly reduce the amount of rainwater that would otherwise run off an impervious roof surface [N3-F3]. They are especially valuable where space constraints limit other stormwater management practices [N3-F3]. In this context, green roofs are not a standalone solution but one element of an integrated system that includes other green infrastructure such as permeable pavement, bioretention, bioswales, and detention basins [N6-R1].

The trade-offs between flood reduction, water quality, and other benefits are important. Green roofs are clearly positioned as stormwater management tools, but their benefits depend on design, installation, and management. The evidence shows that retention and detention capacity are affected by media depth, vegetation, and design [N4-R2][N5-F4]. At the same time, green roofs can provide additional benefits beyond flood reduction, such as improving water quality, reducing building energy use, and increasing the durability of the roof [N3-F3]. However, these benefits come with practical constraints: green roofs require proper structural loading capacity, proper vegetation, and management of drought and saturation conditions [N3-F3][N4-R2].

The evidence also suggests when green roofs are most valuable. They are most valuable in dense urban areas with large roof areas and where impervious surfaces dominate [N3-F3]. They are especially effective when the goal is to reduce peak discharge and delay runoff, as shown by the Singapore case study’s 64% peak discharge reduction and 34-minute delay in time to peak [N2-F2]. In contrast, they may be less effective under extreme rainfall events or when installation factors are inadequate, such as shallow media depth or poor vegetation management [N4-R1][N4-R2][N2-F2].

### 4) How modeling helps quantify and compare green roof flood mitigation

Modeling is a key tool for quantifying green roof flood mitigation. The evidence shows that green roof performance is often modeled using SWMM and related LID controls [N5-F4]. One study simulated storm water performance using SWMM with Low Impact Development (LID) Controls, and noted that the model consists of many parameters for a particular layer of green roofs [N5-F4]. Another study found that SWMM can simulate runoff from green and grey roofs with a good fit between observed and simulated runoff, though in some cases simulation results were unsatisfactory and the Nash coefficient had negative values [N5-F4]. This suggests that model inputs include rainfall, green roof media properties, vegetation, and drainage layer characteristics, but also that model assumptions and calibration are important for accuracy [N5-F4].

Model results can be used to compare green roofs against other infrastructure. The evidence indicates that green roofs can “better manage peak flows in the most critical events” when detention-based practices are incorporated [N5-R2]. It also notes that green and grey roofs can equally reduce the maximum flow by 17% in one study [N5-R5]. This implies that models can compare green roofs with other stormwater control measures, such as detention basins and permeable pavement, and that the relative effectiveness may vary depending on the event and design [N5-R2][N5-R5]. The modeling evidence also shows that model results can be sensitive to assumptions and parameter choices, as the SWMM study found that the complexity of the LID module did not improve accuracy and that further research was needed to determine the role of roof slope, vegetation cover, and drying processes [N5-F4].

Modeling is especially useful for identifying scale-dependent and design-dependent effects. The scale dynamics study finds that green roof drainage area has the greatest impact on peak runoff reduction, and that retention and peak reduction decrease with increased rainfall volume [N4-R1]. Another source reports that the addition of just 3.8 cm of storage can result in a 38.6% reduction in peak discharge for a rainfall depth of 50 mm [N7-R3]. This shows that modeling can reveal how design choices—such as media depth, storage capacity, and roof area—change flood mitigation outcomes. The evidence also indicates that modeling can help compare rooftop-scale performance with larger catchment effects, as the Singapore study used a 9.4 ha subcatchment to scale up the green roof effects [N2-F2]. Overall, modeling helps quantify green roof flood mitigation by predicting peak flow, comparing with other infrastructure, and identifying how design and scale affect performance [N5-F4][N5-R2][N5-R5][N4-R1][N7-R3][N2-F2].

### 5) Synthesis: how green roofs help reduce peak water flow and flooding risk

Putting these findings together, green roofs reduce peak water flow and flooding risk during heavy rainfall in urban areas by acting as a layered stormwater buffer. First, they intercept and store rainfall, delaying runoff and reducing immediate runoff volume [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R5]. Second, they lower peak discharge and shift runoff timing, which reduces the intensity of flow entering drainage systems during intense rainfall [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Third, the evidence shows that these benefits are measurable in real-world urban studies, including the Singapore case study, where peak discharge was reduced by 64% and the average time to peak was delayed by 34 minutes [N2-F2].

However, the benefits are not automatic. They depend on design, installation, and management. Green roofs are most valuable in dense urban areas with large roof areas and when the goal is to reduce peak discharge and delay runoff [N3-F3][N2-F2]. They are less effective under very high rainfall volumes or when installation factors such as media depth are inadequate [N4-R1][N4-R2][N2-F2]. Modeling helps quantify these effects, compare green roofs with other infrastructure, and identify how scale and design influence performance [N5-F4][N5-R2][N5-R5][N4-R1][N7-R3][N2-F2].

In short, green roofs help reduce peak water flow and flooding risk by temporarily capturing and delaying stormwater, thereby reducing the immediate volume of runoff and the intensity of peak discharge [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-F2]. Their value is strongest in urban settings where impervious surfaces dominate and where they can be properly designed and managed [N3-F3][N4-R2]. But their effectiveness is conditional: it depends on rainfall intensity, roof design, media depth, vegetation, and the broader urban stormwater system [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-F4][N2-F2].
